bet.text: An efficient roller floor and indexer, for the most fuel per second.
The stated objective: score 20+ fuel per second with 90%+ accuracy, as far as the Tower.

demand.text: The software group split the game into auto and teleop: simple, efficient autos, and a teleop kept as easy as possible for the drive team.
At the state championship the team says it focused on playing smart, avoiding defense and adapting to every match.

auto.text: A beam break shows whether fuel is still flowing. The robot keeps shooting while it is, then is ready for its next sweep instead of waiting out a timeout.
In a state final an opponent parked in the trench blocked its second pass, worth at least 40 fuel by an analyst's estimate.

cycle.text: It shoots from almost anywhere in the alliance zone and feeds almost anywhere in the neutral zone.
In one Chelsea playoff match, an analyst says, it dumped whole hoppers back, angled into a corner where a fixed shooter can collect, turn slightly and shoot, and herded fuel with its bumpers.

endgame.text: In a state final it and 7769 took the fuel in front of the opponents' hub, so a large bump robot got little from its last trip, an analyst says.

gave_up.text: The intake, the robot's "fighting face", is very prone to breaking. At about 113 lb there was little weight to spare, so most things were made light.
Autos that scored a lot were upset when other robots hit it.
A forum poster says 7407's defense on 27 and 1114 in Archimedes beat the otherwise stronger alliance.

changed.text: The shooter was retrofitted into a robot not designed for it. A belted roller in the feed path shoved balls down and jammed, so it now spins freely. Autos were restructured after hits from other robots.
In build week 5 the first functional climb prototype was done for the practice robot.

outcome.text: 83-6-0 in official play; finalist in the Archimedes division; ranked 26 by championship OPR (269.27, Archimedes).

solves.text: Collect fuel with the part of the robot that takes the hits

facts.text: Main roller has two Kraken X44s at about 2.5:1
A free-spinning carbon fiber roller sits on top, with three passive tubes inside
The team's undated tech documentation differs: rollers on one Kraken X60 and the intake driven by one Kraken X44
Polycarbonate rollers covered in grip tape, a rigid aluminum intake head and SRPP arms
A WCP Throughbore encoder gives position; absolute encoders keep control accurate through power cycles
Built to be very easy to fix

cost.text: Deploy speed is limited by its chain

facts.text: Driven passively by the intake
3D printed sliding system; impact-resistant polycarbonate walls
A net and polycarbonate flaps let the hopper expand vertically
Enough storage in the hopper to meet the scoring needs was a stated goal of the chassis and intake subteam

solves.text: Speed fuel up into a three-wide shooter

facts.text: Two Kraken X60s run it, one at the bottom and one near the back by the indexer
Rollers are polycarbonate; five of them have cat tongue; roller size
Dead axles with 3D prints funnel the fuel into three-wide
The front, angled part runs 1:1 and the back about 17:19, so fuel speeds up into the shooter
A free-spinning roller only stops fuel from being caught above it
PEM nuts make rollers easy to remove and install

cost.text: The same roller, when belted, shoved fuel down and jammed

solves.text: Shoot from almost anywhere in the alliance zone within a tight space and weight

facts.text: One steel 3 in drum on four Kraken X60s; two hood rollers run from the same motors
The 1 in hood rollers spin about two times as fast as the drum, to keep backspin low
One Kraken X44 adjusts the hood, rack and pinion style
Almost all of it is SRPP plastic, for weight
Carbon fiber structure lets the hood take hits from the trench
Compression changes along the path: about 5/8, 3/8 and a final 1/2 (units not spoken)
The feeder accelerates fuel first, so the shooter gives only the final boost

The team's undated tech documentation differs from the interview: up to 20 fuel per second through a launcher three fuel wide, wheels on a REV MAXSpline axle, a three-stage collapsible hood that scores and feeds from the front or back, and a Hall effect sensor for hood angle

solves.text: Get the last fuel out of the hopper without the driver thinking about it

facts.text: Commands interrupt each other in three levels: intake deployed and running is highest, a full agitate override by the joystick driver is next, a slow default agitate while shooting is lowest
A high-velocity Motion Magic profile makes the agitation quick

solves.text: Know in auto whether fuel is still flowing

facts.text: Shooting continues while fuel flows past it; when flow stops the next sweep starts

solves.text: Keep a good pose while shooting and while feeding

facts.text: The main Limelight 4 is weighted heavily because the robot shoots in that orientation
Left and right Limelights act as almost one unit with a fused pose estimate while feeding or when the back cannot see
The constantly updated pose sets shooter speed and hood angle
Predicting the future fuel position, with velocity and acceleration, lets it shoot while moving

solves.text: Write an auto path once for all four corners of the field

facts.text: Created in build week 2: one path can be translated to all four corners
Autos were developed with PathPlanner; pathfinding also runs autonomous features in teleop

solves.text: Be fast, highly maneuverable and all-terrain capable (objective)

facts.text: WCP X2ST modules; maximum speed
Frame of 29.5 in by 25 in, for stability, a centered point of rotation and the most hopper volume
Four Kraken X44s steer and four Kraken X60s drive
Wheels of 3.5 in diameter and 1.75 in width, for stability
Skids built into the bumpers help over the bump and protect the swerve motors
Riveted frame, to avoid welding warp; REV Grid tube with riveted gussets
18 motors and one servo on the robot

solves.text: Make room for the roller floor and the shooter

facts.text: All electrical components are mounted on the bottom
The cover that protects them is attached to the bumpers, so its weight counts with the bumpers
Breaker, camera and RSL mounts are 3D printed
An inverted, water-jetted aluminum belly pan holds the electronics
Two CAN buses: a CANivore bus for drivetrain and critical systems, a REV bus for subsystems and sensors

decisions.choice: A floor of connected polycarbonate rollers
Different compressions along the shooter path
decisions.because: the shooter had to fit, as a retrofit, in space the robot already had; testing and benchmarking found almost no effect on the output

decisions.choice: Mount all electronics on the bottom, under a cover on the bumpers
decisions.because: it saves space for the floor and shooter, and the cover's weight goes to the bumpers instead of the robot

decisions.choice: Build in phases: initial prototype, high-fidelity prototype, practice robot, practice robot v2 upgrades and competition robot
decisions.because: it promotes iteration toward the functional objectives

decisions.choice: Let the team choose autos and modify them on the field
decisions.because: hits from other robots had upset autos that scored a lot

decisions.choice: Leave its own depot fuel unscored in the transition period (off-season IRI, first match analyzed)
decisions.because: an analyst reads it as keeping that fuel out of the opponents' reach
